core_principles.text: Focus on lowering your body while keeping your front knee aligned over your ankle with your shin remaining nearly vertical.
Step forward far enough so both knees form approximately 90-degree angles at the bottom of the movement.
Keep your chest lifted, shoulders relaxed, and spine in a neutral position throughout the exercise.
Tighten your abdominal muscles as though preparing for a gentle impact before beginning each repetition.
Press firmly through the heel of your front foot to rise back to standing.
Lower your body slowly, pause briefly at the bottom, and return to the starting position with smooth, controlled movement.
Keep your head in a neutral position by looking straight ahead throughout the repetition.
Warm up prior to lunges with several minutes of light cardio and dynamic stretches such as leg swings, walking knee raises, or bodyweight squats.
Keep your feet approximately hip-width apart throughout the exercise.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the front knee to extend well past the toes during the lunge.
Taking a step that is too short or too long, disrupting balance and form.
Leaning the torso too far forward while lowering into a lunge.
Performing lunges without proper core activation.
Relying heavily on the back leg to push back up to the starting position.
Rushing through repetitions rather than executing controlled movements.
Looking down at your feet while performing lunges.
Placing one foot directly in front of the other as if walking on a tightrope.

consequences.text: Allowing the front knee to extend well past the toes places unnecessary stress on the knee joint.
Leaning the torso too far forward shifts the workload away from the legs and places unnecessary strain on the lower back.
Lacking proper core activation increases the risk of losing balance and compensating with poor posture.
Relying heavily on the back leg to return to standing reduces the workload on the front leg glutes and quadriceps.
Rushing through repetitions reduces muscle engagement and increases the likelihood of losing balance.
Looking down during lunges causes the neck and shoulders to round forward, reducing proper body alignment.
Placing feet directly in line with each other makes balancing much more difficult during the lunge.
